candidates.name: Ada package private declarative region
candidates.reason: An explicit private declaration region could provide a model for restricting Swift implementation declarations to their enclosing class or extension while allowing related declarations to remain in one file.
candidates.application_scope: Language visibility rules and the syntax separating API from implementation.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Ada grants access within a package and its child units; adapting this to Swift requires defining the class/extension boundary. The community rendering warns that it is unverified.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened manual index https://ada-lang.io/docs/arm/ identifies the Reference Manual as the 2022 Edition, later than 2016-04-01; no earlier version was opened.

candidates.name: Pony type-private fields
candidates.reason: Pony's type-private fields offer a compiler-defined rule that can protect each type's implementation state from neighboring types independently of their physical file placement.
candidates.application_scope: Privacy of stored implementation state and a visible marker with language semantics.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Underscore-prefixed methods have package/module visibility, so this mechanism alone does not supply class-private helper methods or Swift extension rules.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened Classes and Methods tutorial pages are live and show no publication date; the copyright footer does not establish the privacy rules' availability by 2016-04-01.

raw_response:
I found two transferable mechanisms through opened awesome catalogues. Their application to Swift below is a design inference, not an implementation or deployment result. Neither has pre-cutoff availability established by the opened evidence.

1. **Ada package private declarative region** — https://ada-lang.io/docs/arm/AA-7/AA-7.1/
   An explicit private declaration region could model visibility limited to a class or extension while related declarations stay in one file. The documented boundary includes the package and child units, so Swift would need its own boundary rule. Discovery: https://github.com/ChessMax/awesome-programming-languages. Evidence date: **post-decision**; the opened manual index identifies the **2022 Edition** (https://ada-lang.io/docs/arm/). This community rendering warns that it is unverified.

2. **Pony type-private fields** — https://tutorial.ponylang.io/types/classes
   Type-private fields provide a language rule for protecting implementation state from neighboring types independently of file placement. A leading underscore carries privacy semantics. The transfer is limited: private methods are package/module-visible, so the mechanism does not by itself protect class-only helper methods or define Swift extension access (https://tutorial.ponylang.io/expressions/methods). Discovery: https://github.com/dckc/awesome-ocap. Evidence date: **unknown**; no dated version establishing availability by 2016-04-01 was opened.

The catalogue search also reached Scala, Kotlin and C++ resources, but usable primary evidence for their relevant visibility rules was not obtained within the 25-open budget, so they are not returned as candidates.

budget.accounting: Every open or click attempt is counted, including failures, redirects and the repeated catalogue anchor. Searches and find operations are recorded separately; find inspected already opened documents.

limitations: This is an internal separate-context model translation run, not a human study.
Only the assigned baseline rules and C29 prefix were read from the repository; no gold, other runs, repository history or target proposal was accessed.

Discovery was restricted to awesome-list queries and opened catalogues. Non-catalogue search spillover was ignored for discovery; external pages were used only to verify already catalogue-discovered candidates.

The 2022 Ada evidence is retained as later evidence. Pony evidence remains date_status=unknown; post_decision=false for unknown means no confirmed later publication date, not proof of pre-cutoff availability.

The Ada evidence is a community rendering of the language reference manual, with an explicit unverified-output warning; its primary-standard text was read but not cross-checked against another edition.
Pony's method boundary is broader than its field boundary; the fetched Classes page says package and the refreshed Methods page says module.
Six page-open attempts failed: five blocked requests and one timeout. The hosted Kotlin catalogue returned only a JavaScript-required shell.
Scala, Kotlin and C++ language-rule candidates were not included because relevant primary verification was incomplete.
No specific excluded target proposal was recognized in returned snippets or opened content. Model pretraining knowledge cannot be erased and memory leakage is not controlled.
No compiler was run and no claim of deployment or demonstrated utility is made.
